ISO 7243 WBGT method. WBGT is calculated from the measured temperatures and compared with a reference value based on the workload (metabolic rate). Standard work clothing is assumed; special clothing such as protective coveralls needs a correction. Results near the limit call for a detailed assessment (ISO 7933).
Thermometer with a wet wick in natural air movement.
Black globe (150 mm) measuring radiant heat.
Air temperature shielded from the sun.
Light: seated hand work, light bench work standing, slow walking
Moderate: sustained arm-leg work, wheelbarrow, walking 3.5–5.5 km/h
Heavy: intense arm-trunk work, shovelling, carrying heavy material
Very heavy: near-maximal pace, stairs, running
Acclimatised (working in these conditions for at least 1–2 weeks)
Not acclimatised (new starter, back from leave)

Lifting Fatigue Failure Tool (Gallagher et al., 2017). Every lift during the day accumulates a small amount of fatigue damage in the lower back tissue. Enter the load, horizontal distance and daily count for each lift type; the probability of a high-risk job for the lower back is calculated from the cumulative damage.
Horizontal distance: the largest horizontal distance from the spine to the hands/load during the lift.
Enter load, distance and count for at least one lift.
Damage grows exponentially with moment, so first bring the load closer to the body or reduce the weight in this lift; shortening the distance is more effective than reducing the count.
Reduce daily repetitions with mechanical aids, rotation or batch lifting.
⚠ The publication advises careful interpretation for moments above 100 N·m.

Distal Upper Extremity Tool (Gallagher et al., 2018). Enter the difficulty of each type of exertion on the OMNI-RES scale (0–10) and its daily count; cumulative damage and the probability of disorders for the hand, wrist and elbow are calculated. Assess each arm separately.
OMNI-RES: the worker’s or observer’s rating of “how hard is this force?”. Count per day: total repetitions in the shift.
Enter at least one difficulty and daily count.
Lowering the difficulty by one step cuts the damage to about a third: powered tools, maintenance, better handles, part tolerances.
Reduce daily repetitions or share them between both arms; apply rotation.

Revised Strain Index (Garg, Moore, Kapellusch, 2017). The original Strain Index renewed with continuous variables: force, frequency, duration per exertion, wrist angle and daily duration are entered directly as numbers. RSI ≤ 10 is considered safe, > 10 hazardous. Assess each hand separately.
Percentage of maximum voluntary contraction. Without measurement it can be estimated as Borg CR-10 rating × 10 (e.g. “moderate” 3 → 30%).
Extension (bending towards the back of the hand)
Deviation from neutral. Use the most frequent posture in which the highest force is applied.
Enter force, frequency, duration and hours per day.
⚠ Frequency × duration exceeds the cycle (duty cycle above 100%); check the values.
Lower the force required: powered tools, sharp blades, better handles, part tolerances.
Reduce the number of exertions: split the job, share between both hands, automate.
Shorten forceful holding with a fixture, vice or tool balancer.
Bring the wrist closer to neutral: bent-handle tool, change the workpiece angle.
RSI above the limit of 10; the job should be redesigned.

OCRA checklist, classic version (Colombini and Occhipinti). Scores recovery, frequency, force, posture and additional factors in repetitive upper-limb work and multiplies them by the net repetitive work time. Assess each arm separately. The 2011 revised version (ISO TR 12295) applies recovery as a multiplier; the classic version is used because those tables could not be verified.
